approved: Commonwealth Parole Board (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2025
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill is part of a package that would create an independent Commonwealth Parole Board to decide on the conditional release and supervision of federal offenders and other detained people.
The board would be staffed by experts qualified to assess the risk an offender poses to the community and whether they are suitable for parole.
The package would embed impartiality, independence, transparency and accountability in federal parole decisions, according to the explanatory memorandum.
Establishes a statutory independent Commonwealth Parole Board.
Requires the board to make risk-informed decisions on conditional release and management of federal offenders.
Strengthens integrity standards in federal parole decision-making.

Moved the Commonwealth Parole Board (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2025, making amendments to transfer federal parole decision-making from the Attorney-General to the Commonwealth Parole Board, provide discretion over statutory consideration timeframes and ensure the transition does not disrupt corrective services or law enforcement.

Moved that the Commonwealth Parole Board Bill 2025 and its consequential and transitional provisions bill be referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration after the second-reading debate.

Opposed the Commonwealth Parole Board Bill 2025 and its associated bill, arguing that parole decisions should remain with the Attorney-General rather than an appointed board. Claimed the proposal would weaken ministerial accountability, risk community safety, disadvantage victims and create unnecessary costs of $28.3 million over the forward estimates and $7.3 million per year ongoing.

Supported the Commonwealth Parole Board Bill 2025 and related consequential provisions bill, arguing that an independent expert board would make risk-informed parole decisions focused on community safety, rehabilitation and reintegration. The bills would transfer parole decisions from the Attorney-General, allow limited deferrals and longer reconsideration periods, and provide $28.3 million over four years from 2025-26 and $7.3 million a year ongoing.

Argued that the Commonwealth Parole Board bills would transfer responsibility for federal parole decisions from the Attorney-General to an unelected authority, weaken ministerial accountability, sideline victims, and establish a costly bureaucracy, and said the coalition would oppose them.
